thesis: This episode argues that TSMC's pure-play foundry model is a brilliant strategy that avoids competing with its customers, fostering deep trust and technological leadership. The speaker highlights TSMC's foresight and ability to recover from setbacks, such as initially losing Apple's business to Samsung, to regain market dominance through superior technology development.

claims.quote: Then Don Brooks said, well, tell me one company, one big company that's functionalized, and McKinsey immediately answered Boeing, which is a good answer. Ben: Yeah, except it's not true. Boeing has commercial and government.

claims.claim: Morris Chang mentions Texas Instruments as a company where he had experience as a top manager before becoming CEO at TSMC.
claims.quote: I had a lot of experience at Texas Instruments, but at Texas Instruments I was not a CEO. I was just one of the top managers under the CEO level.

claims.claim: TSMC's pure play foundry business model is brilliant because it avoids competing with customers, unlike integrated design manufacturers.
claims.quote: This is why you started TSMC as a pure play foundry business because you didn't want to compete head-to-head. You said, we should not be an integrated design manufacturer of the design of the chips and the manufacturing.

claims.claim: TSMC has strong technology and customer trust, positioning it well against Intel for Apple's supply needs.
claims.quote: All the characteristics that Apple is looking for in a supplier, technology at that time, we thought we were almost at par with Intel. Almost. In fact, I thought we were at par with Intel at that time. Manufacturing, I thought we were better than Intel. And customer trust, we thought that our customers trusted us more than Intel's customers trusted Intel.

claims.claim: TSMC made a significant trade-off by delaying 16nm development to focus on 20nm for Apple, but eventually regained the lead.
claims.quote: The trade-off of accepting the 20-node technology was that we delayed our 16 node development. Then Samsung came up with the 16. They had lost the 20 business so they went ahead of us in the 16-nanometer department.

claims.claim: TSMC's ability to see things before they happen in the foundry business demonstrates its brilliance and foresight.
claims.quote: I actually see a lot of things before they actually happen.

claims.claim: TSMC successfully developed its own 16nm technology and captured most of Apple's requirements after initially losing the business to Samsung.
claims.quote: We developed our own 16 about half a year later. Most of Apple's 16-nanometer requirements still belonged to us. Most.

claims.claim: TSMC's business with Qualcomm increased rapidly after 1997-1998, indicating strong customer relationships and market position.
claims.quote: Our business with Qualcomm, the business that Qualcomm gave us pretty rapidly increased after that 1997–1998 period.
